end_card.title: Effector Lab
lines: Describe a robot job. Get a tested tool setup, with replays and evidence.
Everything shown is simulated. Verify on hardware.
end_card.credit: Built with Nebius Token Factory, NVIDIA Nemotron and Nebius Serverless Jobs

thumbnail.title: Effector Lab
thumbnail.subtitle: Describe a job. Get a tested tool setup.

shots.on_screen: Home: the headline and the tote replay in the hero, then the four stages of how it works.
shots.voiceover: Robot jobs take several steps. Open a lid, put two parts in, close it. One tool rarely suits every step, so teams guess, then find out on the robot.

shots.on_screen: Plan a job: pick the returns-tote example, press Plan, and the recorded planner calls appear one by one until the plan is valid.
shots.voiceover: Effector Lab starts with plain words. You describe the job, and Nemotron, running on Nebius Token Factory, plans it as objects, steps and pass criteria a simulator can check.
shots.caption: Nemotron on Nebius Token Factory · recorded calls, replayed

shots.on_screen: The checks: the problems the first call sent back, then an impossible lift on step 2 turns the step red, and a sensible one makes the plan valid again.
shots.voiceover: Code checks every rule, from reach to what each step must measure. If a plan breaks one, Nemotron gets the problems back and repairs it. You can edit any step.

shots.on_screen: Show all data on the returns tote: why candidates were ruled out before physics (among them a nut runner and a tamper pad), then the success matrix, every screened tool against every step with pass rates and ruled-out cells, scrolled slowly down to the tamper pad and the vacuum frame.
shots.voiceover: Then physics decides, in simulation. Every tool tries every step it could do, from grippers to vacuum frames, a nut runner and a tamper. Misfits are ruled out.
shots.caption: Every candidate × every step · simulated

setup.text: a nut runner turns a fastener

shots.on_screen: The tote's answer in one sentence (a single servo gripper, 8 of 8 runs, also the best single tool) with its fidelity and 'Simulated, verify on hardware' badges, then 'Why this setup' and the comparison with the best single tool: no second tool earned its place.
shots.voiceover: The answer follows an integrator's rules. One tool is the default, and a second tool has to earn its place. For the tote, one servo gripper finished eight of eight runs, and nothing beat it.
shots.caption: One tool by default · simulated, verify on hardware

shots.on_screen: The solar job's replay at 2x, from just before the first tool change: the 'Changing tool' card covers the change to the suction cup, the cup starts the clamp, then a second card covers the change to the nut runner.
shots.voiceover: Every replay is recorded physics that passed a quality gate. Parts are set down, and every pair of objects is checked for overlap. A tool change shows as a card.
shots.caption: Recorded physics · quality-gated · simulated

shots.on_screen: The solar job's answer (a tool change, vacuum area frame then suction cup then nut runner, 7 of 8 runs) and the task in plain words, then its step cards: place the panel, insert the clamp, tighten it.
shots.voiceover: An eight-kilogram solar panel goes onto its rails, then its clamp is tightened to six newton metres, a nut runner's job. A tool change, vacuum frame, suction cup, then nut runner, finished seven of eight runs.
shots.caption: Tool change: vacuum frame > suction cup > nut runner · 7 of 8 runs · simulated

shots.on_screen: The tile job's replay at 1x from just before the head switch: the tile set on its bed by the vacuum frame, the switch to the tamper pad on the same head, then the press that levels it.
shots.voiceover: A floor tile goes onto fresh adhesive and is tamped level, within one millimetre, at no more than sixty newtons. A two-tool head, vacuum frame plus tamper, finished eight of eight.
shots.caption: Within 1 mm · at most 60 N · two-tool head, 8 of 8 runs · simulated

shots.on_screen: The hotel job's replays at 2x: the recommended two-tool head's angular-jaw gripper pulls the door open, then the scrubber jumps to the last step, where its 25 mm suction cup places the parcel in the tray; beside it the best single tool, stopped at the button.
shots.voiceover: A hotel delivery presses an elevator call button, opens a door and places a parcel. A two-tool head, a suction cup and an angular-jaw gripper, finished eight of eight runs.
shots.caption: Two-tool head: suction cup + angular-jaw gripper · 8 of 8 runs · simulated

shots.on_screen: Evidence: the use-case benchmark card with its three held-out rows and the job, then the dated note on what the first version could not test.
shots.voiceover: Does it hold up? Our first version took a pre-registered test on Nebius Serverless Jobs. On thirty-two held-out conditions per job, its picks finished thirty-two, thirty-two and ten. The best single tool finished none of ninety-six.
shots.caption: First version, held out: 32/32 · 32/32 · 10/32 against 0/96 for the best single tool

shots.on_screen: The finger experiment: the S1 table and the best-so-far chart.
shots.voiceover: In a second pre-registered test, Nemotron with simulator feedback found good gripper fingers in fewer designs than random search.
shots.caption: Pre-registered: p = 0.0011

shots.on_screen: The use-case atlas: 'What the research says' with the one-tool share and the bars by domain, then the browser of 95 jobs.
shots.voiceover: The use-case atlas lists ninety-five real jobs with the setup an integrator would expect, as research estimates. Sixty-nine of them need one tool.

shots.on_screen: {{pending: hosted runner live}} Plan a job: the key field and the hosted run starting, with its daily cap shown.
shots.voiceover: It is all open source. Plan a job here with your own NVIDIA or Token Factory key, and the physics runs on our capped Nebius jobs.

fallback.on_screen: Run it yourself: the install commands, then the Docker commands.
fallback.voiceover: It is all open source. Run the search on your own machine with one command, or in Docker.

shots.on_screen: End card: the name, the links, the simulation caveat, the AI voice-over note and the credit line.
